cards.headline: From Scattered Automations to a Unified System
cards.body: Individual automations are useful. But a complete Automation Operating System is transformative. Today you assemble everything — workflows, agents, monitors, and documentation — into one cohesive system that you can manage, share, and scale from a single dashboard.
cards.statLabel: unified system controlling all your automations

cards.headline: Your Automation OS Components
cards.body: A complete system has five layers:
bullets: Registry: A list of every automation — name, purpose, trigger, platform, status
Documentation: Each automation has a "spec" — what it does, why, and how to fix it
Monitoring: Real-time health dashboard (built in Lesson 26)
Version history: Record of changes made — what was updated and when
Playbooks: Step-by-step instructions for common issues (restart, debug, rebuild)

cards.headline: Building Your Automation Registry
cards.body: Create a master document (Notion, spreadsheet, or doc) with one row per automation:
bullets: Name: What you call it (e.g., "Client Email Triage")
Platform: Where it lives (Zapier, Make, n8n, custom)
Trigger: What starts it
Key actions: What it does in 1 sentence
Owner: Who's responsible if it breaks
Last reviewed: When you last checked it still works

cards.headline: The Monthly Automation Review
cards.body: Every month, spend 30 minutes reviewing your OS: Are all automations still needed? Any that haven't triggered in 30 days — do they still serve a purpose? Are there manual tasks that crept back in? What new automation opportunities exist? This review prevents bloat and keeps your system lean and effective.

cards.headline: Build Your Automation Registry
cards.body: Create a Notion page or spreadsheet titled "My Automation OS." Add columns: Name, Platform, Trigger, What It Does, Status (active/paused/broken), Last Reviewed. Fill in every automation you've built during this course (should be 10+). Add a monthly reminder to review this registry. Paste the completed registry into AI and ask: "What gaps do you see? What processes am I still doing manually that could be automated?"

quiz.question: What is an "Automation Registry"?
options: A master list of all your automations with key details
quiz.explanation: An Automation Registry is your master reference — listing every automation with its name, platform, trigger, purpose, owner, and status so you have complete visibility.

quiz.question: You should only review your automation system when something breaks.
quiz.explanation: A monthly proactive review prevents problems — checking if automations are still needed, identifying manual tasks that crept back, and spotting new opportunities.

quiz.question: What should you do with an automation that hasn't triggered in 30 days?
options: Evaluate whether it still serves a purpose and pause/remove if not
quiz.explanation: Inactive automations should be evaluated — they may be handling a rare but important event, or they may be obsolete. Review and decide: keep, update, or remove.

lessons.title: Scale & Delegate
lessons.subtitle: Teach others your systems, scale beyond yourself, and automate the automation.

cards.headline: The Ultimate Automation: Making Yourself Optional
cards.body: You've built an incredible automation system. But the final frontier isn't automating more tasks — it's making the entire system run without you. Teaching others, documenting everything, and creating self-healing workflows means your system generates value even when you're on holiday.
cards.statLabel: your system works even when you don't

cards.headline: Scaling Your Automations
cards.body: Take your system from personal to team-wide:
bullets: Template your workflows: Turn personal automations into reusable templates others can deploy
Create shared folders: Organise automations by department/function so teams find what they need
Build for others: Create automations for teammates that save THEM time too
Standardise: Use consistent naming, documentation, and structure across all workflows
Measure ROI: Track total time saved across the team — build the business case

cards.headline: The Delegation Framework
cards.body: Teaching others to use (and build) automations:
bullets: Document: Every automation has a one-page spec (what, why, how, troubleshooting)
Record: Create 2-minute Loom videos showing how each automation works
Train: Run a 30-minute "automation basics" session for your team
Empower: Give team members access to build their own simple automations
Support: Create a #automations Slack channel for questions and sharing

cards.headline: Self-Healing Systems
cards.body: The pinnacle of automation: systems that fix themselves. Auto-retry on failure. If retry fails → try alternative method. If alternative fails → create a support ticket for human review. If no human responds in 4 hours → escalate to manager. The system handles 95% of issues without you ever knowing there was a problem.

cards.headline: Create Your Automation Handover Document
cards.body: Pick your 3 most important automations. For each, write a one-page spec: (1) What it does in one sentence. (2) Why it matters (what breaks if it stops). (3) How it works (trigger → steps → output). (4) How to fix it (common errors + solutions). (5) Who owns it. Share this with a colleague and ask: "Could you maintain this if I was unavailable?" Their answer reveals documentation gaps.

quiz.question: What is the "ultimate automation" according to this lesson?
options: Making your system run without you
quiz.explanation: The ultimate automation is making yourself optional — systems that are documented, delegated, and self-healing so they generate value 24/7 regardless of your involvement.

quiz.question: Self-healing automations should immediately alert a human for every single error.
quiz.explanation: Self-healing systems first try to fix themselves (retry, alternative method) and only escalate to humans when automated recovery fails — handling 95% of issues automatically.

quiz.question: What should an automation handover document include?
options: What it does, why it matters, how it works, how to fix it, who owns it
The full source code of every connected app
quiz.explanation: A complete handover document covers: purpose, importance, workflow description, troubleshooting guide, and ownership — everything someone needs to maintain it independently.
